CT.notes: Municipal (not county) tax collector sales — Connecticut has no county government.

DE.statute: Delaware Code Title 9 (varies by county) / Title 25 for monition process

DC.returns: Up to 18% per annum plus fees

FL.notes: Two-stage system: county tax lien certificate sale, then a separate tax deed sale if the lien is unredeemed and the holder applies.

IN.notes: County-run certificate sales; unsold liens may go to a commissioners' sale.

IA.notes: County treasurer auctions (bid-down of percentage of parcel acquired).

KS.redemption: None once judicial foreclosure completes (roughly 3+ years of delinquency)
KS.notes: Judicial in-rem foreclosure process run by the county; sheriff's sale for the deed.

LA.statute: Louisiana Revised Statutes Title 47, Subtitle III
LA.notes: Parish-level sales (Louisiana uses parishes instead of counties).

ME.redemption: 18 months from lien filing, before deed recorded
ME.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer after redemption period
ME.notes: Municipality (not county) holds the tax lien and can foreclose administratively.

MD.redemption: 6 months minimum before foreclosure action can start; up to 1 year+
MD.notes: County/city auctions; purchaser must file a foreclosure action to clear title.

MA.redemption: 6 months from sale/taking (often extends in practice via litigation)
MA.notes: Municipality sells the tax title or takes it directly; purchaser forecloses via Land Court.

MI.redemption: Forfeiture/foreclosure process ends redemption rights before auction (roughly 2 years of delinquency)
MI.notes: County (or state, via Dept. of Treasury in some cases) runs the foreclosure and auction.

MN.redemption: 3 years from judgment (5 years for homestead/ag land)
MN.notes: County auctions land after the state forfeiture process completes.

MS.notes: Chancery clerk runs the county sale; unredeemed liens convert to a deed to the purchaser.

MO.redemption: 1 year (2 years for some parcels) from sale
MO.returns: 10% per annum plus 8% on subsequent taxes paid
MO.notes: County collector auctions; purchaser must petition for a collector's deed after the redemption period.

MT.notes: County treasurer assigns liens; purchaser applies for a tax deed after redemption expires.

NE.returns: 14% per annum statutory, bid-down at some county auctions
NE.notes: County treasurer certificate sales, typically in March.

NV.redemption: None once county trustee's deed issues (2-year delinquency threshold before that)
NV.notes: County treasurer holds the property in trust, then auctions after the redemption window closes.

NH.redemption: None post-deed; New Hampshire moved to a deed/lien-hybrid tax lien statute in some municipalities post-Tyler v. Hennepin reforms
NH.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer in most municipalities
NH.notes: Municipality (not county) manages the process; procedures vary by town since 2022 legislative changes.

NJ.redemption: 2 years from sale (statutory minimum before foreclosure)
NJ.returns: Up to 18% per annum, bid down at auction; additional 2–6% penalty on larger liens
NJ.notes: Municipal-level (not county) lien sales; investor forecloses via the Superior Court to obtain title.

NM.redemption: None once the state Property Tax Division auctions the property (3-year delinquency threshold)
NM.notes: State-run (not county) auction through the Property Tax Division.

NY.redemption: Typically 2 years, varies widely by county/municipality charter
NY.returns: Varies — many counties use in-rem deed foreclosure rather than lien certificates; some (e.g., select NYC-area jurisdictions) sell liens
NY.statute: New York Real Property Tax Law Art. 11
NY.notes: Highly county/municipality-specific; check the local charter before assuming a lien or deed process applies.

NC.redemption: 10 days upset-bid period after each high bid, not a traditional redemption
NC.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer, subject to upset bids
NC.statute: North Carolina General Statutes Ch. 105, Art. 26
NC.notes: Judicial (mortgage-style) foreclosure with an upset-bid process that can extend the sale for months.

ND.redemption: 3 years from first delinquency before county takes title; county then auctions the deed
ND.returns: N/A once auctioned (county takes title first, no certificate sold to public)
ND.notes: County takes tax deed itself after the redemption period, then sells at auction — no investor-held lien certificate stage.

OH.redemption: 1 year from lien certificate sale (varies); forfeiture-to-deed track has no redemption once complete
OH.returns: Lien: up to 18% per annum, county-set
OH.notes: Larger counties run certificate (lien) sales, often via a private servicer; smaller counties more commonly go straight to a forfeited-land (deed) sale.

OK.redemption: None once the 2-year resale (deed) process completes; the initial certificate has no per-investor lien sale in most counties
OK.returns: 8% per annum accrues on the underlying tax certificate held by the county
OK.notes: County holds a certificate itself for 2 years, then holds a public resale (deed) auction — unlike states where investors buy the certificate directly.

OR.redemption: None once the county forecloses (3-year delinquency threshold before that)
OR.notes: County holds title via judgment, then auctions; some counties allow direct sale of tax-foreclosed land.

PA.redemption: None in most counties for upset/judicial sales; limited redemption (90 days) survives in specific home-rule counties (e.g., Philadelphia, in narrow cases)
PA.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer in the large majority of counties
PA.statute: Pennsylvania Real Estate Tax Sale Law, 72 P.S. §5860.101 et seq.
PA.notes: Two-tier process in many counties: upset sale (subject to liens) then judicial sale (liens stripped) for unsold parcels.

RI.returns: 10% penalty in year one, plus 1% per month after, plus costs
RI.notes: Municipal (not county) tax sale; Rhode Island has no active county government.

SC.returns: 3–12% per annum depending on when redeemed, tiered quarterly
SC.notes: County-run; often described as a 'redeemable deed' since a deed is issued at sale but subject to the redemption right and interest.

SD.redemption: 3 years from sale (varies for some parcel types)
SD.statute: South Dakota Codified Laws Ch. 10-23 to 10-25
SD.notes: County treasurer certificate sales; purchaser applies for a treasurer's deed after redemption expires.

TN.redemption: 1 year from the court's confirmation of sale (courts have discretion to extend)
TN.returns: 10% per annum statutory penalty on redemption
TN.notes: Judicial (Chancery Court) sale process run at the county level.

TX.redemption: 2 years for homestead/ag/mineral properties; 6 months for all other property
TX.returns: 25% penalty in year one, 50% in year two (homestead/ag); 25% flat for the 6-month category
TX.statute: Texas Tax Code Title 1, Subtitle E, Ch. 34
TX.notes: County (via constable/sheriff) sale; high statutory redemption penalties make this one of the most closely watched markets.

UT.redemption: None once the county auctions (4-year delinquency threshold before that)
UT.notes: County-run May auctions after the statutory delinquency period runs.

VT.redemption: 1 year from sale (town may set differently by charter)
VT.notes: Municipality-level (town), not county, since Vermont counties have no independent government function here.

VA.redemption: Right to redeem up until the court confirms the sale, not after
VA.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer once confirmed
VA.notes: Judicial in-rem sale process; independent cities function as county-equivalents in Virginia.

WA.redemption: None once the county treasurer's deed issues (3-year delinquency threshold before that)
WA.notes: County treasurer runs the foreclosure and auction directly.

WV.notes: State Auditor's office (not the county) administers delinquent-land sales for most counties.

WI.redemption: None once the county forecloses (roughly 2 years of delinquency before that)
WI.notes: County in-rem foreclosure process; some municipalities also handle their own special assessments separately.

WY.notes: County treasurer certificate sales, typically in the second week of August.

redemption.extendedFor: homestead and agricultural-use property (2 years); all other property is 180 days

TX.assessmentBasis: Texas requires appraisal at 100% of market value as of Jan 1 (Tex. Tax Code § 23.01).
caveats: The 180-day vs 2-year window turns on the property's use at the time of sale, which the sale list does not state — treat any homestead-looking residential parcel as potentially 2-year.
Purchaser takes subject to the redemption right; you cannot deliver insurable title until it expires.
The 25% is a flat penalty, not annual interest.

redemption.extendedFor: redemption stays open indefinitely until the purchaser forecloses it by statutory notice (barment)

GA.assessmentBasis: Georgia assesses at 40% of fair market value (O.C.G.A. § 48-5-7).
caveats: The 12-month period is a minimum, not an expiry — the redemption right persists until you serve barment notice, so budget for that process.
A redeemable deed conveys no right of possession during the redemption period.

FL.assessmentBasis: Florida assesses at just value, but Save Our Homes / Amendment 1 caps compress assessed below market on long-held homesteads.
caveats: Governmental liens (municipal code enforcement, some special assessments) can survive a Florida tax deed — check the specific municipality.
Federal tax liens survive with a 120-day IRS right of redemption after the sale.
Most title insurers will not insure until a quiet title action completes, and many not until a year after recording.

redemption.extendedFor: interest is bid down at auction from a 16% statutory maximum

AZ.assessmentBasis: Arizona uses Limited Property Value, which lags full cash value and is capped at 5% annual growth (A.R.S. § 42-13301).
AZ.statute: A.R.S. Title 42, ch. 18 (tax liens and foreclosure)
caveats: Arizona sells liens, not deeds — the usual outcome is redemption with interest, not property ownership.
Taking title requires a separate judicial foreclosure after 3 years, at additional legal cost.
16% is the maximum; competitive auctions routinely bid the rate into low single digits.

MI.assessmentBasis: Michigan state equalized value is 50% of true cash value by constitution (Mich. Const. art. IX, § 3); taxable value may be lower still. The SEV published with these auction listings is taken from the delinquent tax year that was foreclosed upon, so it is typically several years stale — in a rising market it understates current value, and in a falling one it overstates it.
MI.statute: MCL 211.78 et seq. (general property tax act, foreclosure)
caveats: Michigan's foreclosure judgment cuts off prior liens and the owner's interest, so title is comparatively clean — quiet title is often unnecessary.
Valuations here derive from a stale SEV, not comps. Treat the computed ARV as a starting point and override it with real comparable sales before bidding at the ceiling.
Rand v. Rand / Hall-era excess-proceeds rules mean former owners may claim surplus; this does not affect the buyer's title.

redemption.extendedFor: owner-occupied principal residence of 1–6 dwelling units (30 months); most other property redeems at 24 months

bidDown.note: 81.4% of recorded Cook County liens cleared at a 0% penalty bid. Institutional buyers take these for the deed remainder rather than the interest, so expected return on the redemption path is close to zero and the real thesis is acquisition.

IL.assessmentBasis: 35 ILCS 200/9-145: property outside Cook County is assessed at 33⅓% of fair cash value.

17031.basis: Cook County Classification Ordinance: Class 2 residential is assessed at 10% of market value, not the statutory 33⅓%.

IL.statute: 35 ILCS 200, Art. 21 (sale and redemption); Art. 22 (tax deed)
caveats: The penalty is bid DOWN from an 18% ceiling, so the tiers above are a best case, not an expectation. Recorded Cook sales cleared at a 0% median and a 1.88% mean across 64,526 liens — price an Illinois lien on the acquisition thesis, not the interest.
Cook County assesses residential at ~10% of market value, not the statutory 33⅓%. The county override above handles this; parcels in other Illinois counties use the statutory ratio.

Title is perfected by petition for tax deed under Art. 22 rather than a classic quiet-title action. The cost and duration here are market practice for that proceeding plus any curative work an insurer requires, and are not fixed by statute.
Redemption runs 24 months for most property and 30 months only for an owner-occupied principal residence of 1–6 units. Commercial, industrial and vacant non-residential stay at 24.
Cook also runs a scavenger sale for long-delinquent parcels under different minimum-bid rules (35 ILCS 200/21-145 et seq.) that this entry does not model.

CA.assessmentBasis: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 401: property is assessed at full cash value, so the statutory ratio is 1.0.
CA.derivedArvCaveat: California assesses at full cash value, but Proposition 13 fixes the base year and factors it forward at up to 2%/yr. On a long-held parcel the assessed value can sit far below market, so an ARV derived from it understates the property — get comparable sales before bidding.
CA.statute: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 3691–3731 (tax-defaulted property sales)
caveats: No post-sale redemption. The owner's right ends at 5pm on the last business day before the sale, so the deed conveys without that overhang.
Proposition 13 means assessed value systematically understates market value on long-held parcels. Do not treat a ratio-derived ARV as an appraisal in California.
RTC § 3711 makes the tax deed presumptively valid, so quiet title is optional rather than required — but most title insurers still want it before writing a policy.
Some non-residential commercial property reaches power-to-sell after 3 years of default rather than the usual 5 (RTC § 3691).
Recorded San Diego sale lists mark pre-sale cures as 'REDEEMED'. That is the owner paying before the auction, not a post-sale redemption, and it is quarantined in the copilot's label rules.

resolvedRules.survivingLiens: Buying a lien does not convey the property — it's a certificate of purchase. The owner can redeem at any point before a treasurer's deed is applied for (after 3 years), so no lien is 'cleared' at the certificate stage. Once a treasurer's deed does issue, most private liens are cleared, but state/federal liens can survive.
resolvedRules.quietTitle: Arizona treasurer's deeds are widely regarded as weak title; most investors pursue a quiet title action before attempting to sell or insure the property, even though it isn't always a strict legal prerequisite to holding the deed.
